title: Flying with Inoperative Equipment — 91.213(d) Flowchart

required_knowledge_points.title: The 91.213(d) Four-Step Exclusionary Flowchart
required_knowledge_points.why: Every DPE presents an inoperative equipment scenario. The applicant who says 'I'd just placard it inoperative' without running the four-step analysis fails. The process must be methodical, sequential, and documented.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: When an aircraft without an approved MEL has a broken piece of equipment, the pilot uses the four-step exclusionary flowchart of 14 CFR 91.213(d) before placarding. If the broken item answers YES to ANY of the four questions, the aircraft is GROUNDED until it is repaired. Step 1 — Is the item required by the aircraft's Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS)? Step 2 — Is the item listed in the aircraft's Equipment List or KOEL in the AFM for the intended operation? Step 3 — Is the item required by 14 CFR 91.205 or any other applicable regulation? Step 4 — Does any active AD require the item to be operational?
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### When to Use This Flowchart
- Aircraft **without an approved MEL** with an inoperative piece of equipment
- **If the item answers YES to ANY step → aircraft is grounded** until repaired

### The Four Steps (14 CFR 91.213(d))

**Step 1 — Type Design:**
- Is the item required by the aircraft's **Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS)**?

**Step 2 — Equipment List / KOEL:**
- Is the item listed as required in the aircraft's **Equipment List** or **Kinds of Operation Equipment List (KOEL)** in AFM Section 2 for the intended flight?

**Step 3 — Regulations:**
- Is the item required under **14 CFR 91.205** (ATOMATOFLAMES / GRABCARD) or any other applicable Part 91 rule for the specific operation?

**Step 4 — Airworthiness Directive:**
- Does any active **AD** require the item to be operational?

### If All Four Steps Answer NO:
- The item may be deactivated, **placarded 'INOPERATIVE'**, and the flight may proceed — only after a final safety determination per 91.213(d)(4)

required_knowledge_points.title: Deactivation, Placarding, and the Maintenance Line
required_knowledge_points.why: Students know the flowchart but don't know that how you deactivate the item determines who must perform the deactivation — a flip of a switch vs. a maintenance action. This distinction is on the checkride.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Once an item passes the 91.213(d) flowchart, it must be physically remediated. Two options: (1) Removed from the aircraft — almost always requires an A&P mechanic. (2) Deactivated and placarded 'Inoperative' — the placard must be placed adjacent to the control or indicator. If deactivating the equipment is as simple as turning a switch to OFF, the pilot may do this. If deactivating requires cutting a wire, pulling or collaring a circuit breaker, or any action that crosses into maintenance territory, a certificated A&P mechanic must perform and log the deactivation under 14 CFR 43.9.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Two Remediation Options
- **Remove the item** — almost always requires an **A&P mechanic** (affects W&B, requires logbook entry per 14 CFR 43.9)
- **Deactivate and placard 'INOPERATIVE'** — placard must be placed **adjacent** to the control or indicator

### Who Can Deactivate — The Maintenance Threshold
- **Pilot may deactivate** if it is as simple as turning a **switch to OFF**
- **A&P mechanic required** if deactivation involves:
  - Cutting or disconnecting wiring
  - Pulling and **collaring a circuit breaker behind a panel**
  - Any physical maintenance action beyond a switch or knob
  - Action must be logged per **14 CFR 43.9**

### Deferral Is Not Indefinite
- Per **14 CFR 91.405(c)** and the **De Joseph (2017)** and **Peri (2018)** FAA interpretations:
- At the **next required inspection** (Annual or 100-Hour), the mechanic must formally address the deferred item: **repair, remove, or inspect and re-document**

required_knowledge_points.title: KOEL vs. 91.205 — The Most Restrictive Rule Wins
required_knowledge_points.why: The most common error in 91.213(d) scenarios is stopping at 91.205 without checking the KOEL. The KOEL is in Section 2 (Limitations) of the AFM and is a legally binding limitation that can be more restrictive than 91.205.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: 14 CFR 91.205 (ATOMATOFLAMES for Day VFR) is the federal floor for equipment requirements. However, the aircraft manufacturer's Kinds of Operation Equipment List (KOEL) in Section 2 of the AFM is a legally binding operating limitation under 14 CFR 91.9. The KOEL can require items that 91.205 does not. The pilot must comply with the more restrictive requirement. Scenario: 14 CFR 91.205 does not require an anti-collision light for Day VFR, BUT the Cessna 172 KOEL lists it as required. The aircraft is grounded for Day VFR because the KOEL is more restrictive.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### 14 CFR 91.205 — The Federal Floor (ATOMATOFLAMES)
**A**irspeed indicator · **T**achometer · **O**il pressure gauge · **M**agnetic direction indicator · **A**ltimeter · **T**emperature gauge (liquid-cooled) · **O**il temperature · **F**uel gauges · **L**anding gear position indicator · **A**nti-collision lights (post-1996 manufacture) · **M**anifold pressure (altitude engines) · **E**LT · **S**afety belts

### KOEL — Legally Binding Limitation (AFM Section 2)
- Listed in **Section 2 (Limitations)** of the FAA-approved AFM
- A legally binding **operating limitation** per **14 CFR 91.9** — can be **more restrictive** than 91.205
- The pilot must comply with whichever is more restrictive

### Classic Exam Trap
| Equipment | Required by 91.205? | Required by Cessna 172 KOEL? | Aircraft Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anti-collision light | No (Day VFR) | **Yes** | **Grounded** |

> Applicant who stops at 91.205 and declares flight legal **fails the scenario** — must always check the KOEL

required_knowledge_points.title: Legal vs. Safe — The Final Determination Requirement
required_knowledge_points.why: Checkride failure mode: applicant completes the four-step flowchart, declares the equipment 'not required,' placards it, and considers the flight legal without making the mandatory final safety determination under 91.213(d)(4).
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Even after successfully passing all four steps of the 91.213(d) flowchart, the flight is NOT automatically cleared for departure. 14 CFR 91.213(d)(4) imposes a final requirement: a certificated pilot or mechanic must determine that the inoperative equipment does not constitute a hazard under the anticipated operational conditions. This is a subjective, holistic safety assessment — not a rubber stamp. The pilot must apply the PAVE checklist specifically to the missing equipment.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### The Final Gate — 14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)
- Even after passing all four flowchart steps, the flight is **NOT automatically cleared**
- A certificated **pilot or mechanic** must determine the inoperative equipment does **not constitute a hazard** for the anticipated operation
- This is a **holistic safety judgment** — not a rubber stamp after checking the boxes

### Apply PAVE to the Inoperative Item
- **Pilot:** Does the missing item increase PIC workload beyond current proficiency?
- **Aircraft:** Does losing this system critically degrade redundancy?
- **enVironment:** Does the weather, airspace, or terrain amplify risk from the missing item?
- **External Pressures:** Are passengers or schedule causing rationalization of a real risk?

### The Legal ≠ Safe Rule
- Example: A broken **airspeed indicator** is NOT on the 91.205 VFR Day list → technically legal to fly
- BUT for a low-time pilot in turbulent conditions → could be **catastrophically unsafe**
- The final determination under 91.213(d)(4) is where the pilot **must make this call explicitly** before departure

lesson_overview:
## Flying with Inoperative Equipment — 91.213(d) Flowchart

You walk out to the aircraft for your checkride flight and discover the landing light is burned out. Can you fly? What if it's the OAT gauge? What if it's the VSI? What if it's the attitude indicator? Each of those answers is different — and the DPE is going to ask you one of them. The framework that governs all of these decisions is the 91.213(d) decision tree, and it applies to every piece of equipment in the aircraft.

**Step one: Is there an MEL?** The first branch of the tree: does this aircraft have an FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List? An MEL is a document, specific to the aircraft type and operator, that lists every system and specifies which components may be inoperative and under what conditions. MELs are standard on commercial operators and some flight schools with established maintenance programs. If there is an MEL: follow it exactly. If the MEL says the inoperative item requires a placard and a write-up but permits flight, you're legal to fly. If the MEL says the item must be repaired before flight, the aircraft is grounded.

**Step two: No MEL — apply the four-step check under 91.213(d).** For Part 91 operations without an MEL, the regulation provides a four-question test for any inoperative equipment. Work through them in order. If the answer to any question is YES, the aircraft is grounded. The four questions are: Is it required by the Type Certificate Data Sheet? Is it required by the AFM Equipment List or KOEL? Is it required by 91.205 or another regulation? Is it mandated by an active AD?

**ATOMATOFLAMES — the VFR day list from 91.205(b).** This acronym covers the legally required instruments and equipment for VFR flight during the day: Airspeed indicator, Tachometer, Oil pressure gauge, Magnetic direction indicator (compass), Altimeter, Temperature gauge (liquid-cooled engines), Oil temperature, Fuel gauges, Landing gear position indicator (retractable), Anti-collision lights (post-1996), Manifold pressure (altitude engines), ELT, Safety belts. Items NOT on this list that many students assume are required: VSI, attitude indicator, turn coordinator, OAT gauge.

**The KOEL trap.** Many applicants stop the analysis at 91.205 and declare the flight legal. That is wrong. The aircraft manufacturer's Kinds of Operation Equipment List (KOEL), in Section 2 of the AFM, is a legally binding operating limitation. The KOEL can require items that 91.205 does not. The Cessna 172 KOEL, for example, lists the anti-collision light as required for Day VFR — even though 91.205(b) does not. If the anti-collision light is inoperative, the aircraft cannot fly Day VFR — not because of 91.205, but because the KOEL is more restrictive, and the FAA-approved AFM is a binding limit. Always check the KOEL.

**The final determination — legal does not equal safe.** Even after passing all four steps, the flight is not automatically authorized. Under 91.213(d)(4), the pilot or mechanic must make an active determination that the inoperative item does not constitute a flight hazard for the anticipated operation. A broken ASI is not on the VFR day required list — but flying into actual IMC with a broken airspeed indicator is not safe. That determination must be made explicitly, applying PAVE to the specific missing item in the specific conditions of the flight.

**The checkride trap:** Two classic DPE setups: (1) Ask about an item that IS on the 91.205 list — the correct answer is 'the aircraft cannot fly without it.' (2) Present an item that passes 91.205 but is on the KOEL. Students who stop at 91.205 fail. The DPE is testing whether you apply the full framework, not just one step of it.
